stem:
A woman at 35 weeks has a major placental abruption. The obstetric and anaesthetic teams are resuscitating her and preparing urgent birth. She received 1 L of crystalloid before blood was taken. Her blood pressure at booking and on arrival was normal and urinalysis showed no protein. She develops oozing from cannula sites. Results:

| Test | Result | Laboratory reference range |
|---|---:|---|
| Platelets | 58 × 10⁹/L | 150–400 × 10⁹/L |
| Prothrombin time | 23 seconds | 11–14 seconds |
| Fibrinogen | 0.8 g/L | 2.0–4.0 g/L, non-pregnant |

She has no previous bleeding disorder or anticoagulant exposure.

Which complication best explains this pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation from the abruption
options.explanation: Very low fibrinogen, prolonged prothrombin time and low platelets with oozing after a major abruption indicate consumptive coagulopathy.

options.label: B
options.text: Dilutional coagulopathy from the crystalloid resuscitation
options.explanation: One litre of crystalloid cannot lower fibrinogen from pregnancy levels to 0.8 g/L or platelets to 58; the pattern indicates consumption.

options.label: C
options.text: Gestational thrombocytopenia unmasked by the haemorrhage
options.explanation: Gestational thrombocytopenia is mild and does not prolong the prothrombin time or deplete fibrinogen.

options.label: D
options.text: HELLP syndrome presenting without hypertension or proteinuria
options.explanation: HELLP can occur without hypertension, but no haemolysis or raised liver-enzyme evidence is supplied. Profound hypofibrinogenaemia and prolonged prothrombin time after major abruption support DIC.

options.label: E
options.text: Immune thrombocytopenia with bleeding from the abruption
options.explanation: Immune thrombocytopenia lowers platelets alone and does not prolong the prothrombin time or deplete fibrinogen.

context: Major placental abruption can cause DIC, with falling platelets, prolonged clotting times and depleted fibrinogen.
